Part two of a series about AI, individual agency and Future of Work
AI can help us create value. It can also help us win the wrong race.

8 min read
Just now

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Artwork by Author. Mass production creates noise. Deliberate creation becomes signal.If you haven’t read Part 1, The Flood Before the Filter, I’d recommend starting there. This essay builds on the ideas introduced in it.
Lately I have noticed that polished content does not impress me the way it used to.
I can come across a well-designed image or a neatly written post, understand its point and keep scrolling. There may be nothing obviously wrong with it. It is clear, organised and probably useful to someone, but it feels familiar before I have even finished reading it.
This does not mean I have become good at detecting AI. Most people have not. Research suggests that people can sometimes distinguish AI-written material from human writing, but their ability varies considerably. In other studies, especially with images, people have performed only a little better than chance.
What we may be getting better at recognising is sameness.
The familiar openings, predictable arguments, smooth summaries and conclusions that sound important without leaving us with much to think about. A human may have made them. AI may have made them. Usually both were involved in some way.
The source is not always clear, but the repetition is becoming easier to feel.
The flood is already here
In the first part of this series, I used Gresham’s Law to describe what happened when AI made content much cheaper to produce.
Gresham’s Law is normally used for money. When stronger and weaker forms of money are treated as though they have the same value, people tend to keep the stronger money and spend the weaker one. The lower-quality money becomes more visible in everyday circulation.
Something similar happened online. An article someone developed over several weeks and an article generated in a few minutes both appear as posts in the same feed. The platform does not show the work, doubt or research behind them. It shows two finished rectangles on a screen.
AI adoption also happened very quickly. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index estimated that generative AI reached around 53 per cent population-level adoption within three years, faster than the early adoption of personal computers or the internet. The data varries regionally but hollistically it is on the rise.
We do not have a reliable number for how much of the internet is now AI-generated, so I do not think we should pretend to know. But smaller markets give us an idea of what happens when production becomes easier.
A Stanford study of a stock-image marketplace found that after generative AI arrived, total image production rose by 136 per cent and the number of active artists increased by 47 per cent. At the same time, the production of non-AI images fell by 15 per cent, while the number of active non-AI artists fell by 29 per cent.
More work entered the market, but the people already doing the work also faced more pressure.
I do not think this is temporary. AI is now part of search engines, writing software, design platforms, offices and phones. There is no realistic future in which everyone agrees to stop using it.
That is why I am not writing this series to argue against AI. The flood has already happened. The question is what we decide to contribute now.
What Thiers’ Law does and does not promise
Thiers’ Law is often described as the reverse of Gresham’s Law. When people can freely choose between different kinds of money, they may eventually move towards the one that holds its value better.
Applied to information, the hopeful version would be that people will become tired of cheap content and return to thoughtful work.
That may happen, but I would not treat it as a guarantee.
Low-quality work can succeed. A person can copy popular formats, publish constantly, manufacture expertise and build an audience before anyone asks whether they understand what they are talking about. They may gain followers and make money. They may even become an example that other people are encouraged to follow.
The worrying part is not only that someone might lose the rat race. They might become very good at winning it.
Good work does not rise automatically. People must be able to recognise it, trust it and choose it. Even then, speed and emotional certainty may still beat care.
Research also does not show that people always prefer human work.
In five experiments involving 1,722 participants, researchers compared human advice with advice produced by ChatGPT. People’s reactions depended on the quality of the answer, whether its source was disclosed and how authentic it felt.
Another study on ethical advice found that 72.6 per cent of participants initially preferred advice from a human. After seeing the quality of the AI advice, that figure fell to 53.2 per cent. When the source was hidden, it fell to 46.3 per cent.
So the simple claim that human work will always win is not supported by the evidence. Sometimes AI produces a better answer. Sometimes people like the answer but become less comfortable with it after learning where it came from. Sometimes the label matters more than the actual quality.
This makes the choice more interesting, not less.
The same tool can serve two different intentions
Someone can use AI to understand a difficult subject, question their own argument, organise research or explain something more clearly.
It can remove some of the mechanical work and give a person more time to think about what deserves to be included. It can also help someone find gaps, compare sources and turn a rough idea into something another person can understand.
But the same tool can be used to create articles around popular keywords, imitate another writer’s structure or present expertise that the creator does not have.
A person can generate advice they have never tested, cite research they have not read and speak with confidence about subjects they barely understand. With enough polish, it can still look useful.
Both creators may use the same AI model. Both may produce attractive work, and both may succeed for a while.
The difference is not whether AI was used. The difference is what the person was trying to do with it. Were they trying to become more useful, or only trying to appear useful?
Trust is harder to produce
A 2025 Reuters Institute study found that many people who had encountered AI-generated search answers trusted them at least somewhat, but they still worried about accuracy, sourcing and transparency.
That feels close to how many of us now use AI. We trust it enough to ask, but not always enough to stop checking.
There is another problem. The appearance of evidence can sometimes be enough to earn trust.
In one study of AI search, citations and reference links increased people’s trust even when some of the references were wrong or invented. People were responding partly to the appearance of research rather than verifying whether the research was real.
Creators can exploit the same weakness.
They can add impressive numbers, mention unnamed studies or place references below a graphic. Most readers will not check every claim, so false confidence may work.
Real trust is slower. A reader returns and discovers that the source exists, the numbers were represented honestly and the creator corrects mistakes rather than hiding them. Over time, the reader learns whether that person is worth listening to.
AI can copy the appearance of this trust much faster than it can help someone earn it.
Even the platforms are adjusting
Platforms are not banning AI-created work. They are trying to reduce material that is repetitive, mass-produced or made mainly to manipulate the system.
In July 2025, YouTube renamed its “repetitious content” monetisation policy to “inauthentic content.” It clarified that repetitive or mass-produced material may not qualify for monetisation, while creators can still use AI tools if the finished work remains original and adds value.
Google’s spam policies use a similar principle. Its rules against scaled content abuse apply whether content is created by humans, automation or a combination of both. The important question is whether the material was made to help users or mainly to manipulate search rankings.
Platforms will not enforce these rules perfectly. Useful work will still be overlooked, and empty work will still spread.
But the distinction is important. It is not human versus AI. It is value versus the appearance of value. A lot of good content appears in our feeds but have you ever wondered was this idea timed rightly…. was there a need for this. This is the appearance of value , we have to face moving forward.
We still decide what we add
Nobody knows exactly what the future of creative work will look like.
Audiences may become better at filtering. AI-generated content may become almost impossible to identify. Trusted individuals and smaller communities may become more valuable because people need shortcuts for deciding what deserves attention.
Cheap content may also continue winning large amounts of attention.
All of these things can be true at once.
Individual agency does not mean controlling the system. It means deciding how to act inside a system we did not design and cannot completely escape.
We can use AI to produce more than we understand, or we have the option to understand more before we produce.
We can use it to imitate trust, or to make our work more worthy of trust.
We can treat people as traffic, or remember that there is a person on the other side of the screen who gave us some of their limited attention.
Thiers’ Law suggests that people may move towards what holds value when they can recognise it and freely choose it. Perhaps that will happen with information too.
But it will not happen automatically, and it does not remove our responsibility.
The future of work will probably not be divided between people who use AI and those who refuse it. It may be divided between people who use it to create value and people who use it to manufacture the appearance of value.
Both may gain attention. Both may make money.
That is what makes the decision difficult.
The danger is not only that we might lose the new race.
It is that we may win it and realise that nobody has a reason to trust what we built.
While writing this, I kept thinking about kind Midas story. Midas wished that everything he touched would turn to gold. He got exactly what he wanted. Then he discovered he could no longer eat, drink, or embrace the people he loved.
We wished for effortless production, and we got it.
Now we have to decide why we create in the first place.
AI will help us produce more of whatever we value.
If we value attention above all else, it will help us chase attention.
If we value understanding, trust and being useful to other people, it can help us build those too.
The tool has already arrived.
What it amplifies is still up to us.
